def: The R-enantiomer of albuterol, a short-acting beta-2 agonist bronchodilator used for asthma and COPD, with the goal of fewer tachycardia side effects.
Airway narrowing triggered by vigorous exercise, causing cough, wheeze and dyspnea minutes after activity, especially in cold dry air. Prevented with a short-acting beta-2 agonist beforehand.
Conjunctivitis in the first month of life acquired during delivery. Chemical irritation occurs within a day, gonococcal within 2 to 5 days (severe, purulent) and chlamydial at 5 to 14 days.
Infection by Toxocara canis or cati roundworm larvae from ingesting soil contaminated with dog or cat feces, causing visceral or ocular larva migrans with eosinophilia.
Systemic Toxocara larval migration through organs, causing fever, hepatomegaly, cough and marked eosinophilia, mostly in young children who eat soil.
Development of female characteristics in a male, such as gynecomastia and reduced body hair, from estrogen excess or androgen deficiency or resistance.
Inflammation of the maxillary sinus, causing facial pain and pressure over the cheek, purulent nasal discharge and fever; usually from viral infection, sometimes bacterial.
A bedside scoring system using vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, consciousness) to detect clinical deterioration.
A direct connection between an arteriole and venule that bypasses capillaries, regulating blood flow in places such as the skin of the fingers, where it is important for temperature control.
Extra teeth beyond the normal set, such as mesiodens at the midline of the upper jaw. Associated with cleidocranial dysplasia and Gardner syndrome.
An antihistamine and mast cell stabilizer, used in eye drops for allergic conjunctivitis.
A compound in which a glucose sugar is bound through its anomeric carbon to another molecule; cardiac glycosides like digoxin are examples of glycosides.
A cyanogenic glycoside in apricot kernels and bitter almonds that releases cyanide when hydrolyzed; marketed as laetrile and can cause cyanide poisoning.
The cytokine receptor on eosinophils that binds interleukin-5, promoting their growth and survival. Targeted by benralizumab for severe eosinophilic asthma.
Infarction of the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, causing loss of motor function, pain and temperature below the lesion, while dorsal column (vibration, proprioception) function is spared.
Persistent industrial chemicals (formerly used in coolants and insulators) that accumulate in fat and cause skin lesions like chloracne, liver toxicity, and developmental and endocrine effects.
An ascending flaccid paralysis caused by a toxin from engorged female ticks (Dermacentor), resolving after the tick is removed.
A topical and intranasal corticosteroid of medium to high potency used for dermatoses, allergic rhinitis and asthma.
Bipolar neurons in the olfactory epithelium whose axons pass through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb. They are replaced throughout life.
Chest pain or pressure from myocardial ischemia when oxygen demand exceeds supply, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin in the stable form.
The acinar and ductal portion of the pancreas that secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum; comprises about 98 percent of the organ.
Membrane-bound vesicles or inclusions in cells storing secretory products or enzymes, such as neutrophil, mast cell and platelet granules.

Lung infection by Aspergillus invading tissue and vessels in neutropenic or immunosuppressed patients, causing fever, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis and nodules with a halo sign. Treated with voriconazole.
A childhood epileptic disorder with acquired aphasia (verbal auditory agnosia) after normal language development, with EEG abnormalities worsening in sleep.
An anticoagulant that chelates calcium in blood collection tubes and a urinary alkalinizer; also a buffer used as an antacid before anesthesia.
A falsely low platelet count from platelet clumping in EDTA-containing tubes; resolved by repeating the count in a citrate or heparin tube.
A group of inherited blistering skin diseases from defects in skin anchoring proteins (keratins, laminin, collagen VII), causing blisters after minor friction.
A growth factor that binds the EGF receptor to stimulate epithelial proliferation; implicated in Menetrier disease and some tumors.
A family of cytokines. TGF-beta suppresses inflammation, drives fibrosis and induces IgA class switching, while TGF-alpha stimulates epithelial growth.
Emergency airway technique in which a sedative and a rapid-acting paralytic (such as succinylcholine) are given together to speed intubation and lower aspiration risk.
A chemokine released from platelet alpha granules that binds heparin. Antibodies against heparin-PF4 complexes cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
Recording of the heart's electrical activity from the body surface, used to diagnose arrhythmias, ischemia and conduction disease.
Chronic venous insufficiency after deep vein thrombosis, from damaged venous valves, causing leg swelling, aching, skin pigmentation and ulcers. Also called post-thrombotic syndrome.
Rapidly progressive skin necrosis and hemorrhage from small vessel thrombosis and DIC, seen in meningococcemia, sepsis and protein C or S deficiency.
Chronic inflammation of the tissues supporting the teeth, causing gum recession, bone loss and tooth loosening, driven by plaque bacteria like Porphyromonas gingivalis.
Muscle contraction that generates force without changing the muscle's length.
The joint between the patella and femoral trochlear groove. Maltracking causes patellofemoral pain syndrome (anterior knee pain).
A benign, blood-filled, expansile bone lesion of children and young adults, appearing as a soap-bubble lucency on imaging, often with USP6 rearrangements.
The skull base compartment holding the temporal lobes and pituitary; contains the foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum and the foramen lacerum.

A condition where one functional copy of a gene produces too little protein for normal function, so a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation causes disease (e.g., Marfan syndrome, familial hypercholesterolemia).
A coccidian protozoan (Cystoisospora belli) that causes watery diarrhea in AIDS patients, with acid-fast oocysts in stool. Treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

A coccidian protozoan (Cyclospora cayetanensis) acquired from contaminated produce, causing watery diarrhea; oocysts are acid-fast and larger than Cryptosporidium. Treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
A CNS stimulant that increases release of dopamine and norepinephrine, used for ADHD and narcolepsy. Causes insomnia, appetite loss and elevated blood pressure.
Surgical removal of the rectum, performed for rectal cancer, ulcerative colitis or severe inflammatory disease.
Acute joint inflammation from monosodium urate crystals depositing, classically in the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.
Drugs such as roflumilast and apremilast that raise cAMP in inflammatory cells by blocking PDE4; used in severe COPD, psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis.
Formation of pus from tissue inflammation, typically from pyogenic bacteria.
Growth of new blood vessels into the normally avascular cornea, due to hypoxia, infection or inflammation (as in contact lens wear).
A clonal proliferation of plasma cells, including monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, multiple myeloma and plasmacytoma.
Needle aspiration of fluid from the middle ear through the tympanic membrane, to obtain a culture in refractory otitis media.
Structural airway changes from chronic inflammation, such as smooth muscle hypertrophy, basement membrane thickening and mucus gland enlargement, as in chronic asthma.
An amphibole asbestos type linked to asbestosis, pleural plaques, mesothelioma and lung cancer.
The serpentine (white) form of asbestos, with curly fibers; the most commonly used type.
Straight, needle-like asbestos fibers (amosite, crocidolite) that penetrate deep into the lung; more strongly linked to mesothelioma than serpentine types.
The blue amphibole asbestos with thin straight fibers, the type most strongly associated with mesothelioma.
The fan-shaped muscle of the temporal fossa that elevates and retracts the mandible. Innervated by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve.
A motor neuron disease variant affecting brainstem cranial nerve nuclei, causing dysarthria, dysphagia and tongue atrophy with fasciculations; often progresses to ALS.
Insulin-secreting cells in the center of the islets of Langerhans, which also make amylin and C-peptide. Destroyed in type 1 diabetes.
The blood supply to the digestive organs via the celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, receiving about a quarter of cardiac output and draining to the portal vein.
The enzyme that synthesizes acetylcholine from choline and acetyl-CoA in cholinergic nerve terminals. Reduced in Alzheimer disease.
The capsid protein of hepatitis B virus, found only within infected hepatocytes. Anti-HBc IgM marks acute infection, including the core window period.
The presence of virus in the bloodstream.
An oral alkylating agent that methylates DNA, used for glioblastoma; efficacy is better when the MGMT gene is silenced.
Abnormal spine curvature, including scoliosis (lateral), kyphosis (excessive thoracic rounding) and lordosis (excessive lumbar inward curve).
Irreversibly modified proteins formed by non-enzymatic glucose attachment in prolonged hyperglycemia; they cross-link collagen and contribute to diabetic complications.
Surgical cutting of bone, done to realign or lengthen it, such as high tibial osteotomy for knee osteoarthritis.
A collection of fluid in the tunica vaginalis around the testis, which transilluminates. May be congenital from a patent processus vaginalis.
A first-generation antihistamine, used in eye drops and decongestant combinations for allergic conjunctivitis and rhinitis.
An alpha-adrenergic agonist vasoconstrictor used in eye drops to reduce redness and nasal decongestants. Overuse causes rebound congestion.
A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor from islet cells, such as insulinoma, gastrinoma or glucagonoma, often associated with MEN1.
Pinworm infection by Enterobius vermicularis, causing nocturnal perianal itching; diagnosed with the scotch tape test. Treated with albendazole or pyrantel pamoate.
The most common inflammatory myopathy in older adults, causing slowly progressive asymmetric weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps, with rimmed vacuoles on biopsy. Poor response to steroids.
A malignant tumor with neuroendocrine features, such as small cell lung cancer; stains for chromogranin and synaptophysin.
A cascade (RAS, RAF, MEK, ERK) transmitting growth factor signals to the nucleus; mutations in the pathway (e.g., RAS, BRAF) drive many cancers.
Drugs that act on the central nervous system to change mood, thought or behavior, such as antidepressants, antipsychotics and anxiolytics.
A radiotracer taken up by mitochondria-rich tissue, used in cardiac stress imaging and to localize parathyroid adenomas.
A gene encoding a protein, such as a repressor or activator, that controls the expression of other genes.
A fracture involving the pediatric growth plate (physis), classified I to V; types III to V carry a higher risk of growth disturbance.
Peripheral nerve damage from chronic alcohol use and associated thiamine deficiency, causing symmetric painful sensory loss in the feet and legs.
An adrenolytic drug that destroys adrenal cortical cells, used for adrenocortical carcinoma and Cushing syndrome.
Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV hypersensitivity) from urushiol oil in poison ivy, oak or sumac, producing linear vesicular, itchy lesions.
Drugs that relieve itching, such as antihistamines, topical corticosteroids, calamine and menthol.
Substances that cause tissue proteins to contract and dry up secretions, like witch hazel, aluminum acetate and silver nitrate.
A benign tumor of mature ganglion cells and Schwann cells from neural crest, usually in the posterior mediastinum or retroperitoneum in older children and adults.
Inflammation of all layers of the uveal tract (anterior, intermediate, posterior), as in sarcoidosis, Behcet disease and syphilis.
Increased resting muscle tone with resistance to passive stretch, either spasticity (velocity-dependent, upper motor neuron lesion) or rigidity (constant, basal ganglia).
Necrosis of white matter around the lateral ventricles in premature infants, from hypoxic-ischemic injury; leads to spastic diplegia cerebral palsy.
The twelve vertebrae of the upper and mid back, each articulating with ribs through costal facets.
A chloride channel (ClC-2) activator that increases intestinal fluid secretion, used for chronic constipation and constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome.
A calcitonin precursor released in bacterial infection and sepsis; its serum level is used to distinguish bacterial from viral infection and guide antibiotics.
A sympathomimetic amphetamine-like appetite suppressant for short-term obesity treatment.
A sympathomimetic amphetamine-like appetite suppressant for short-term obesity treatment.
A sympathomimetic amine that suppresses appetite, used short term for obesity; causes insomnia and elevated blood pressure.
A skin barrier protein that aggregates keratin filaments in the stratum granulosum. Loss-of-function mutations cause ichthyosis vulgaris and predispose to atopic dermatitis.
The transition before menopause with irregular cycles, hot flashes and falling estrogen, lasting several years.
Spread of tumor through the capsule of a lymph node into surrounding tissue, a marker of more aggressive cancer and worse prognosis.
Infection by Bacteroides, anaerobic gram-negative rods of the gut flora, which cause intra-abdominal abscesses, peritonitis and pelvic infections after bowel injury.
A coronavirus first identified in the Middle East, spread from camels, causing severe pneumonia and kidney failure. Uses DPP4 as its receptor.
A membrane enzyme that converts angiotensin II to angiotensin 1-7 and serves as the entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2.
RNAs made from only part of a viral genome, as in coronaviruses, used to express downstream genes.
Reduction in blood cell and protein concentrations from increased plasma volume, as in pregnancy or IV fluid administration.
A synthetic progestin used in oral contraceptives (including progestin-only pills) and for abnormal uterine bleeding and endometriosis.
The joint between the acromion and the clavicle at the top of the shoulder. Injury is called a shoulder separation.
A blistering agent from blister beetles, applied topically to remove warts and molluscum contagiosum.
A topical antimitotic that binds tubulin, used to treat genital warts.
Agitation, confusion and restlessness upon waking from general anesthesia, most frequent in children.
Persistent headache, dizziness, poor concentration and mood changes lasting weeks to months after a concussion.
A staphylococcal toxin that forms pores in leukocytes, killing them. Panton-Valentine leukocidin is found in community-acquired MRSA causing skin abscesses and necrotizing pneumonia.
The enzyme (24-hydroxylase) that inactivates calcitriol and 25-hydroxyvitamin D by 24-hydroxylation, helping prevent vitamin D excess.
Reactive industrial chemicals in polyurethane and paints; a cause of occupational asthma and the Bhopal disaster (methyl isocyanate).
Acne-like rash of papules and pustules without comedones, a side effect of drugs such as EGFR inhibitors, corticosteroids and lithium.
A transporter in the proximal tubule that reabsorbs filtered phosphate; inhibited by parathyroid hormone and FGF23.
A hormone made by bone cells that increases phosphate excretion and lowers calcitriol. Excess causes hypophosphatemic rickets.
An enzyme from the placenta that degrades vasopressin (ADH); excess in pregnancy can cause transient diabetes insipidus.
Injection of medication, usually corticosteroid or gentamicin, through the eardrum into the middle ear to treat sudden hearing loss or Meniere disease.
Bleeding behind the eye causing orbital compartment syndrome with proptosis, pain and vision loss; needs urgent lateral canthotomy.
The pit viper subfamily (rattlesnakes, copperheads, cottonmouths) with heat-sensing pits; venom causes local tissue damage and coagulopathy, treated with Crotalidae antivenom.
Recurrent itchy vesicles on the palms, soles and sides of the fingers, also called pompholyx, often in atopic patients.
Reversible vasogenic edema of the posterior brain causing headache, seizures, visual changes and confusion; triggered by severe hypertension, eclampsia or immunosuppressants.
Blood in the anterior chamber of the eye, usually after blunt trauma, forming a layer in front of the iris; risk of rebleeding and glaucoma.
Infection of the skin fold around a fingernail or toenail, with painful swelling and sometimes pus, commonly from S. aureus or Candida.
A gram-negative rod of oral flora that causes infections from human bites and clenched-fist injuries, as well as endocarditis.
A supine position with the head lower than the feet; used for central line placement and to improve venous return in hypotension.
A corrosive acid that penetrates tissue and binds calcium and magnesium, causing severe pain, hypocalcemia and arrhythmias. Treated with calcium gluconate.
A neurodevelopmental disorder with persistent difficulty in reading, writing or math despite normal intelligence and adequate instruction.

term: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
def: Failure of the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance after birth, causing right-to-left shunting through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale with hypoxemia.
A nuclear receptor for T3 in the pituitary, liver and other tissues. Mutations cause thyroid hormone resistance with high T4 and non-suppressed TSH.
Reduced tissue response to thyroid hormone, usually from THRB mutations, with elevated T4 and T3 and inappropriately normal or high TSH.
A triangular fibrovascular growth of the conjunctiva over the cornea, associated with UV light exposure. Can distort vision.
Infection by Burkholderia pseudomallei in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, causing pneumonia, abscesses and sepsis. Acquired from contaminated soil and water.
A gram-negative rod in tropical soil and water, causing melioidosis, with bipolar (safety-pin) staining.
Cyclic nausea and vomiting in chronic heavy cannabis users, relieved by hot showers; resolves with stopping cannabis.
An herbal supplement from Piper methysticum used for anxiety, associated with hepatotoxicity.
An herbal supplement taken for memory, with antiplatelet effects that raise bleeding risk.
A long IV catheter inserted through a peripheral arm vein into the superior vena cava for prolonged IV therapy.
Benign cardiac enlargement and slow resting heart rate from conditioning, with increased left ventricular wall thickness and chamber size that regress with detraining.
Pink disease from chronic mercury poisoning in children, with pink painful hands and feet, irritability, sweating and hypertension.
A vasopressin analog that constricts splanchnic vessels, used for hepatorenal syndrome and bleeding esophageal varices.
Measurement of hearing sensitivity across frequencies using tones, used to diagnose conductive versus sensorineural hearing loss.
A high-fat, very low-carbohydrate diet that raises ketone levels; used for refractory childhood epilepsy and GLUT1 or pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency.
Inhibitory receptors for gamma-aminobutyric acid: GABA-A is a chloride channel modulated by benzodiazepines and barbiturates, and GABA-B is a G-protein-coupled receptor targeted by baclofen.
A rare inherited bleeding disorder with prolonged prothrombin time and normal PTT, due to deficiency of the extrinsic pathway factor VII.
The most common peripheral aneurysm, behind the knee, often bilateral and linked to abdominal aortic aneurysm. Risk of thromboembolism and limb ischemia.
Repeated exposure to gradually increasing doses of an allergen to induce tolerance, shifting from IgE to IgG4 and regulatory T cells; used for allergic rhinitis and venom allergy.
A narrow-complex tachycardia arising from the AV junction, often after pediatric cardiac surgery.
A highly toxic dioxin contaminant of Agent Orange that binds the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, causing chloracne and cancer.
A group of persistent toxic organochlorine pollutants produced by combustion and herbicide manufacture; cause chloracne and possibly cancer.
A herbicide mixture used in the Vietnam War contaminated with the dioxin TCDD; linked to soft tissue sarcoma, lymphoma and diabetes in exposed veterans.
The insect order that includes bees, wasps, hornets and ants; their stings cause IgE-mediated anaphylaxis in sensitized people.
An LDL-like particle with apolipoprotein(a) attached, structurally similar to plasminogen. High levels increase risk of atherosclerosis and thrombosis.
The clinical syndrome of prolonged excess cortisol, causing central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, striae, hypertension and glucose intolerance. Most commonly caused by exogenous steroids.
Neurodegenerative loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, causing resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability. Lewy bodies of alpha-synuclein are seen.
Transmural inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the GI tract, often the terminal ileum, with skip lesions, granulomas, fistulas and a cobblestone appearance.
The most common cause of dementia, with progressive memory loss from cortical atrophy, beta-amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles. Linked to APOE e4 and trisomy 21.
Flat epithelial cell of the skin and linings such as the cervix, esophagus and lung airways. Squamous cell carcinoma shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

Trisomy 21, causing intellectual disability, flat facies, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease, and heart defects (endocardial cushion defects). Associated with early Alzheimer disease and leukemia.
Either Paget disease of bone, disordered bone remodeling causing thick, weak bones and elevated alkaline phosphatase, or Paget disease of the breast/vulva, an intraepidermal adenocarcinoma.
Autoimmune hyperthyroidism from antibodies that activate the TSH receptor, causing goiter, exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema.
A tick-borne infection by Borrelia burgdorferi (Ixodes), causing erythema migrans, then facial palsy and carditis, and later arthritis. Treated with doxycycline.

Sickle cell disease, an inherited hemoglobin S disorder from a glutamate-to-valine substitution on the beta-globin chain; hemoglobin polymerizes when deoxygenated, causing hemolysis and vaso-occlusive crises.
45,XO, causing short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, streak ovaries with primary amenorrhea, and coarctation of the aorta or bicuspid aortic valve.
Autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT causing loss of striatal neurons, with chorea, dementia and psychiatric symptoms in adulthood; shows anticipation.
Glial cells of the peripheral nervous system that myelinate a single axon segment each and support nerve regeneration. Derived from neural crest.
Primary adrenal insufficiency, usually autoimmune, with low cortisol and aldosterone causing fatigue, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation.
Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation impairing copper excretion, causing copper buildup in liver, brain and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings), with low ceruloplasmin. Treated with penicillamine.

Medium-vessel vasculitis in children under 5 with fever of 5+ days, conjunctivitis, rash, strawberry tongue, swollen hands and cervical lymphadenopathy. Coronary aneurysms are a complication; treated with IVIG and aspirin.
Large neurons of the cerebellar cortex that provide its only output, inhibiting deep nuclei with GABA. Also, Purkinje fibers are cardiac conduction fibers.
Gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) causing high acid output, severe refractory peptic ulcers and diarrhea. Treated with high-dose proton pump inhibitors; associated with MEN1.
Remnant of the vitelline duct, an outpouching in the ileum, with ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue that can cause painless rectal bleeding.
Severe, drug-triggered mucocutaneous reaction with painful blisters, epidermal detachment (under 10 percent of body surface) and mucosal erosions; larger detachment is toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Autosomal dominant fibrillin-1 defect causing tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens subluxation (upward), aortic root dilation and mitral valve prolapse.
Congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in the distal bowel (RET mutation), so the segment stays contracted, causing delayed meconium passage and a dilated proximal colon.
Interrupted sympathetic supply to the eye and face, causing ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. Causes include Pancoast tumor, carotid dissection and brainstem stroke.
A dendritic antigen-presenting cell in the epidermis, with Birbeck granules (tennis racket shape). Proliferation of these cells causes Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Cushing syndrome caused specifically by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, with high ACTH and suppression of cortisol on high-dose dexamethasone.
The most common lysosomal storage disorder, from glucocerebrosidase deficiency, causing hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain and macrophages with crumpled-tissue-paper cytoplasm.
Autosomal dominant mismatch repair gene mutation (MLH1, MSH2) causing microsatellite instability and early colorectal and endometrial cancer without numerous polyps.
Neurologic disorder of multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic starting before age 18, often with OCD or ADHD.
Hexosaminidase A deficiency causing GM2 ganglioside buildup in neurons, with neurodegeneration, a cherry-red macular spot and no hepatosplenomegaly; more common in Ashkenazi Jews.
